Traditional: Write one question with a short answer you can check at a glance: a word, a number, or a choice of A to D.
Digital: Build it once in Microsoft Forms, a free Microsoft 365 tool for quick quizzes, so you can reuse it with every group.
Accessibility: Show the question on screen and read it aloud. Keep the wording short and plain.
InclusivePractice: Decide before the lesson who you will check in with, so it is never only the learners who volunteer.

Action: Everyone answers at the same time
Traditional: Hand out mini whiteboards. Give a fixed thinking time, then say "boards up" so everyone shows at once.
Digital: With Plickers, each learner holds up a printed card turned to their answer, and you scan the room with your phone. Learners need no device.
Accessibility: Offer large-print cards or a thicker pen to anyone who needs them.
InclusivePractice: Learners who never put a hand up still answer. With Plickers, nobody can see anyone else's answer.

Traditional: Scan the boards. Note the correct answers, the common mistakes and any blank boards.
Digital: Plickers and Forms show who chose what, and save the results for later.
Accessibility: Say the result aloud, for example "about half of you chose B", rather than relying on a coloured chart.
InclusivePractice: You now know who needs support, not only who was willing to speak.

Traditional: Most right: move on. A split: explain again a different way. Few right: re-teach.
Digital: Use the saved results to choose next lesson's starter questions.
Accessibility: Show the correct answer in writing as well as saying it.
InclusivePractice: Follow up quietly with learners who got it wrong, rather than in front of the class.

Traditional: Pick one question from last lesson, one from last week, one from last month and two from earlier in the course.
Digital: Build them as a quiz in Microsoft Forms and turn on automatic marking.
Accessibility: Use a clear font and strong contrast. Forms works with Immersive Reader, which reads text aloud.
InclusivePractice: Mix easier and harder questions so every learner starts the lesson with some success.

Traditional: Learners answer on paper or mini whiteboards, without notes.
Digital: Show a QR code. Learners answer on their phones and see their score straight away.
Accessibility: Allow read-aloud and extra time for learners who need it.
InclusivePractice: Keep it low stakes. No names on the board and no public scores.

Traditional: Share the answers. Learners mark and correct their own.
Digital: The Forms summary shows which question most learners got wrong.
Accessibility: Say each answer aloud and show it in writing.
InclusivePractice: Re-teach the most-missed question to everyone, not only those who got it wrong.

Action: Break the task into small steps
Traditional: Split the task into steps and plan what you will say at each one.
Digital: Use a visualiser, a camera that shows paper or objects on the board, so everyone sees the same detail.
Accessibility: Zoom in, and use a dark pen on plain white paper for strong contrast.
InclusivePractice: Make sure learners who need to see detail have a clear view, or share the visualiser into a Teams meeting.

Traditional: Say why you are doing each step, not only what you are doing.
Digital: Record it. A recorded model becomes a recap learners can replay.
Accessibility: Name what you point at: "the earth cable", not "this one here".
InclusivePractice: Pause after each step and check understanding before moving on.

Traditional: Learners try a similar example while the model is still fresh.
Digital: Leave the finished model on screen, or post a photo of it in the Teams channel.
Accessibility: Share the model as an accessible document or a captioned video.
InclusivePractice: Give a partly completed example to learners who need more support.

Traditional: On printed handouts too, use clear headings so the structure is obvious at a glance.
Digital: In Word, click in the line, then select Home, Styles, Heading 1. Use Heading 2 for sections inside it. In PowerPoint, give every slide a title in the title box.
Accessibility: Text made big and bold is not a heading to a screen reader. Screen reader users jump from heading to heading.
InclusivePractice: Every learner finds their way around a long workbook faster.

Traditional: Read your headings on their own. Do they tell the story of the document?
Digital: Select View, then tick Navigation Pane. Every heading should appear, in order.
Accessibility: Do not skip levels. A Heading 3 sits inside a Heading 2.
InclusivePractice: A clear structure helps learners who find long documents overwhelming.

Traditional: For printed work, check the same things by eye: headings, contrast, and no meaning carried by colour alone.
Digital: Select Review, then Check Accessibility. Fix everything under Errors and Warnings, then save.
Accessibility: The checker finds missing alt text and hard-to-read contrast. It cannot tell you whether your alt text is any good.
InclusivePractice: An empty results list is the floor, not the finish. Look over the file yourself too.

Traditional: Plan each slide around one title and one main idea.
Digital: Add slides with Home, then New Slide, and choose a layout with title and content boxes. They start in the right order.
Accessibility: Boxes you draw yourself are read in the order you added them, not where they sit on the slide.
InclusivePractice: One idea per slide also reduces overload for everyone.

Traditional: Say the slide aloud in the order you would want it heard.
Digital: Select Review, then the small arrow on Check Accessibility, then Reading Order Pane. The top of the list is read first.
Accessibility: In PowerPoint for the web, use Home, Arrange, Selection Pane instead. It runs backwards: the bottom item is read first.
InclusivePractice: Learners using Read Aloud or Immersive Reader get the same order a screen reader does.

Traditional: Title first, then the content in the order you would read it aloud.
Digital: Drag the title to the top of the Reading Order list, then arrange the rest.
Accessibility: Mark decorative pictures as decorative so they are skipped: right-click, View Alt Text, tick Mark as decorative.
InclusivePractice: Built well, the slide works for every learner, not only those looking at it.

Traditional: Ask a colleague to read the slide aloud from top to bottom.
Digital: Run Review, Check Accessibility. Slides with a questionable reading order are listed.
Accessibility: Listen with Narrator, the screen reader built into Windows: press Windows key + Ctrl + Enter to turn it on or off.
InclusivePractice: Fix one real slide today, then use layouts so new slides start right.

Action: Decide whether the image carries information
Traditional: Ask: if the image vanished, would anyone miss anything?
Digital: In Word, PowerPoint, Excel or Outlook, right-click the image and select View Alt Text.
Accessibility: If nothing would be missed, tick Mark as decorative so screen readers skip it.
InclusivePractice: Learners on slow connections, where images do not load, rely on alt text too.

Action: Write what it tells the learner
Traditional: Describe the teaching point in one or two sentences, not what the picture looks like.
Digital: Type it into the Alt Text pane.
Accessibility: Leave out "image of" or "photo of". The screen reader already says it is an image.
InclusivePractice: Learners listening to a document read aloud get the same information as everyone else.

Traditional: For a complex diagram or chart, keep the alt text short and describe it fully in the text on the page.
Digital: Run Review, Check Accessibility. Every image without alt text is listed.
Accessibility: Do not trust automatically written alt text. Read it and rewrite it.
InclusivePractice: Ask a learner who uses a screen reader what helps them most.

Traditional: Keep one master copy of each handout, and give learners copies.
Digital: In your class team, open the General channel, select Files, then open Class Materials. Upload your slides there. Learners can open them but cannot edit or delete them.
Accessibility: Run the Accessibility Checker before you upload.
InclusivePractice: Nobody can change the master copy that everyone else uses.

Action: Name and organise the same way every time
Traditional: Label paper resources with the unit and week.
Digital: Create one folder per unit. Name files with unit, week and topic, for example "Unit 3 Week 2 Brake systems".
Accessibility: Clear, predictable names help screen reader users, who hear file names read out.
InclusivePractice: The same structure on every course means learners only have to learn it once.

Traditional: Tell learners at the start of each lesson exactly where today's material is.
Digital: Pin a "Start here" post: hover over the post, select the three dots, then Pin. Add the current unit's folder as a tab with the + at the top of the channel.
Accessibility: Fewer clicks matter most on phones and for keyboard users. Aim for three or fewer from opening Teams.
InclusivePractice: Learners who find navigation hard are often the first to give up.

Traditional: Keep personal and one-to-one paperwork out of shared folders.
Digital: When sharing a link, select Share, then choose Can view. Use Manage access to see who has access.
Accessibility: Check the link opens on a phone before you post it.
InclusivePractice: Never put one learner's personal or one-to-one record in a space the group can see.

Traditional: Identify the one idea learners must secure before the next part of the lesson.
Digital: Keep hinge questions in a Microsoft Forms bank, tagged by topic, to reuse each year.
Accessibility: Check the question reads clearly in Immersive Reader.
InclusivePractice: Think about which learners usually struggle at this point, and why.

Traditional: Each wrong option should match a misconception you have seen before.
Digital: In Forms, add feedback to each option so learners see why an answer was wrong.
Accessibility: Make the concept the challenge, not the language.
InclusivePractice: Plain wording keeps the question fair for learners with English as an additional language.

Traditional: Everyone answers in under a minute. Decide in seconds what happens next.
Digital: Plickers and Forms show which learners chose each answer, so you can set different next tasks.
Accessibility: Allow extra time where learners need it.
InclusivePractice: Group by misconception, not by ability, so support is targeted rather than labelling.

Traditional: Show a complete, annotated example, step by step.
Digital: Put it on a OneNote page or in the Teams channel so learners can return to it.
Accessibility: Use headings and numbered steps so it is easy to follow with a screen reader.
InclusivePractice: Everyone starts from the same clear model.

Traditional: Give a similar example with the final steps left blank.
Digital: Learners complete it in OneNote or in a Form.
Accessibility: Label every gap clearly.
InclusivePractice: Learners choose how much of the worked example to look back at.

Traditional: Set a similar task with no support on the page.
Digital: Set it as a Teams Assignment with a rubric, a marking grid that shows what good looks like.
Accessibility: Immersive Reader is available on Teams Assignments.
InclusivePractice: Keep scaffolds available on request, rather than removing them for everyone at once.

Traditional: Work through the example on paper as you normally would.
Digital: Record the visualiser or your screen as you go, for example as a Teams meeting recording.
Accessibility: Talk through each step so the recording makes sense without the picture.
InclusivePractice: Learners who were absent, or need more time, get the same explanation.

Traditional: Note the key moments as you teach.
Digital: Open the recording in Stream, trim it and post it in the Teams channel.
Accessibility: Check and correct the automatic captions. They often get names and technical words wrong.
InclusivePractice: Posting in the channel means it works on phones, in the workshop or at home.

Traditional: Next week, ask learners to recall the steps before showing the video.
Digital: Link the recap to a short Forms quiz.
Accessibility: Provide the transcript alongside the video.
InclusivePractice: Learners control the pace: pause, rewind and rewatch.

Traditional: On paper, offer key texts in larger print or on tinted paper, and read key instructions aloud.
Digital: In the Word app, select View, then Immersive Reader, then Read Aloud. In a Teams post, hover over the message, select More options (the three dots), then Immersive Reader.
Accessibility: It works best on documents built with real headings. Run the Accessibility Checker first.
InclusivePractice: Nobody needs a diagnosis or a label to use it.

Traditional: At induction, open a real course resource in front of the group and play a paragraph aloud.
Digital: For Teams Assignments, open the assignment, select Student view, then Immersive Reader, so you see what learners see.
Accessibility: Show text size, spacing, page colour and Line Focus, which shows one, three or five lines at a time.
InclusivePractice: Showing everyone at once means nobody is singled out.

Traditional: Mention it again whenever you set a reading-heavy task.
Digital: Pin a one-line reminder in your team: how to open it, and that it is for everyone.
Accessibility: Use it yourself on the board, so learners see it as normal.
InclusivePractice: Check: ask a learner, "If a document is hard to read, what can you do?"

Traditional: Plan one real task where speaking an answer makes sense.
Digital: In Word, on the Home tab, select Dictate. Anywhere on a Windows computer, press Windows key + H to open voice typing.
Accessibility: A headset microphone works better than a laptop's built-in one, especially in a busy room.
InclusivePractice: You need a microphone, an internet connection and a Microsoft 365 sign-in.

Action: Teach it to the whole group
Traditional: Show everyone at the start of the course, using a real task.
Digital: Set a short task where everyone speaks their answer instead of typing it. Say punctuation aloud, for example "comma".
Accessibility: Dictation also works in PowerPoint and Outlook.
InclusivePractice: Taught to everyone, it becomes a normal way of working, not a special arrangement.

Traditional: Remind learners it is there whenever you set a longer piece of writing.
Digital: Encourage learners to dictate a first draft, then edit it by hand.
Accessibility: If it is not working, check the microphone is not muted, and move somewhere quieter.
InclusivePractice: The exams team can explain what counts as a normal way of working for access arrangements.

Traditional: Face the room and speak clearly. Captions follow speech.
Digital: In PowerPoint, on the Slide Show tab, select Always Use Subtitles.
Accessibility: Check the spoken language setting matches the language you are speaking.
InclusivePractice: Nobody has to ask for captions if they are already on.

Traditional: Repeat key questions from the room so they are captioned too.
Digital: In a Teams meeting, select More actions, then Language and speech, then Show live captions.
Accessibility: Teams does not save captions. Turn on transcription if you need a written record.
InclusivePractice: A transcript helps learners revise afterwards.

Traditional: Choose videos that already have accurate captions.
Digital: For your own videos, generate captions in Stream, correct them, and save the caption file.
Accessibility: Automatic captions get names and technical words wrong. Read them through and correct them.
InclusivePractice: Check: watch with the sound off. Does it still make sense?

Traditional: Plan each slide or section around one idea. Remove anything that does not help learning.
Digital: Use a slide layout, and move detail into the notes or a handout.
Accessibility: Fewer items on a slide also means a shorter, clearer reading order.
InclusivePractice: Clear pages help everyone, and matter most for learners who are struggling.

Traditional: Go one light, one dark: contrast is light against dark, not colour against colour.
Digital: Run Review, Check Accessibility. It flags hard-to-read text contrast.
Accessibility: Aim for at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text.
InclusivePractice: Projectors, sunlight and black and white printing all wash colour out.

Traditional: Add a word as well as a colour, for example "Unit 3 workbook: assessed".
Digital: For anything Office cannot check, use the free WebAIM contrast checker in a browser.
Accessibility: A screen reader never says the colour.
InclusivePractice: About one in twelve men and one in two hundred women are colour blind.

Action: Speak, do not read the slide
Traditional: Talk through the slide rather than reading it word for word.
Digital: Put key words and images on the slide, and the full text in the handout.
Accessibility: Share the slides in advance so learners can follow at their own pace.
InclusivePractice: Learners can listen or read, without trying to do both at once.

Action: Offer more than one way in
Traditional: Explain, demonstrate, and give a written version of the same content.
Digital: Post the slides, a captioned recording and the handout together in the channel.
Accessibility: Every version meets the same accessibility standard.
InclusivePractice: Learners choose the route that works for them that day.

Action: Offer more than one way to show learning
Traditional: Accept a written answer, a spoken explanation or a demonstration, where the qualification allows.
Digital: Teams Assignments accepts documents, audio and video. Dictation and Immersive Reader are available.
Accessibility: Make sure every format can be submitted with a keyboard and a screen reader.
InclusivePractice: Check your awarding body specification for what the evidence must be.

Traditional: Share the success criteria before learners choose a format.
Digital: Use one Teams Assignment rubric for every format.
Accessibility: Write the rubric in plain language.
InclusivePractice: The standard stays the same for everyone; only the route changes.

Traditional: Plan one theory section that learners could meet before the lesson.
Digital: Record an explanation of eight minutes or less and post it in Teams with a three-question Forms check.
Accessibility: Captions on, with the transcript attached.
InclusivePractice: Learners can pause, rewatch and use read-aloud at their own pace.

Traditional: Open the lesson by looking at the check results together.
Digital: The Forms results show who is ready and who needs a recap.
Accessibility: Show results anonymously.
InclusivePractice: Run a short recap group for learners who are not ready yet.

Traditional: Set application tasks and circulate, coaching individuals and groups.
Digital: Learners record their work in OneNote or a Teams Assignment.
Accessibility: Every task comes with an accessible written brief.
InclusivePractice: You spend your time with the learners who need you most.

Traditional: Put a short statement, image or problem on the board. It is not a question.
Digital: Share it in a Teams channel or on a OneNote page where learners can add questions.
Accessibility: Give the focus as text, audio and image.
InclusivePractice: Allow dictation or voice notes, so writing is not a barrier.

Traditional: Learners ask as many questions as they can, write them exactly as asked, do not discuss or judge them, and turn statements into questions.
Digital: Collect questions on a shared Whiteboard or in a Form.
Accessibility: Use Immersive Reader to read the questions back.
InclusivePractice: Anonymous contributions give quieter learners a voice.

Traditional: Learners turn closed questions into open ones and the reverse, then choose their top three.
Digital: Use a Forms ranking question to prioritise as a group.
Accessibility: Keep the final list in plain, structured text.
InclusivePractice: Learners see their own questions shape the next lesson or project.

Action: Use the right tool and keep data safe
Traditional: Choose one dense handout or slide that learners struggle with.
Digital: Open Copilot Chat signed in with your college Microsoft 365 account, not a personal AI tool.
Accessibility: Never paste learner names or personal information.
InclusivePractice: A plainer version helps learners with reading barriers access the same content.

Traditional: Decide who the text is for and what must stay.
Digital: Copy the prompt on this card, paste your text where it says, and send it.
Accessibility: Ask for a reading level and for key terms to be kept and explained.
InclusivePractice: Offer both versions, rather than replacing the original for everyone.

Traditional: Read the output against the original. Is it accurate? Was anything important lost?
Digital: Check names, figures, rules and safety points against a source you trust.
Accessibility: Paste it back into your document and run the Accessibility Checker again.
InclusivePractice: Ask a learner whether the new version is clearer.

Action: Agree a real problem and audience
Traditional: Find a real problem with a real audience, such as a local employer, a school or a community group.
Digital: Set up a project channel in Teams, organised the same way as your course channels.
Accessibility: Share the brief as an accessible document that has passed the Accessibility Checker.
InclusivePractice: Learners choose roles that use their strengths.

Traditional: Plan tasks that need everyone's contribution to succeed.
Digital: Set milestones as Teams Assignments with a rubric.
Accessibility: Each milestone has a clear, written success check.
InclusivePractice: Scaffolds fade as the project goes on.

Traditional: Learners present their solution to the real audience.
Digital: They choose the format: slides, video or a live demonstration.
Accessibility: Presentations meet the same accessibility standard as your own resources.
InclusivePractice: Learners reflect on the project using the 21CLD rubric language.
